summary: The article argues that Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) policies in schools are being adopted faster than the security policy and infrastructure needed to support them. It covers network vulnerabilities, unclear responsibility for device security, privacy concerns, enforcement difficulty, hidden costs, and digital literacy and equity gaps. It concludes that BYOD needs a blend of technology, policy, and education, with coordinated effort among educators, parents, students, and security professionals.
one_line: BYOD policies in schools are outpacing security measures, creating risks around networks, privacy, cost, enforcement, and equity.
key_facts: The article is dated September 12, 2023 and addresses cybersecurity risks of Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) policies in schools.

A report by cybersecurity expert Dr. Karen Zimmermann, published October 3, 2023, found 85% of educational institutions with BYOD policies lack sufficient cybersecurity measures against malware, phishing, and unauthorized access.
BYOD shifts the burden of keeping devices secure and up to date from the institution to individual students and parents, who are often ill-equipped for it.
Emily Rostok, a parent of a high school senior, said in a September 28, 2023 interview: "I'm not a computer person—I trust the school to keep things secure."
Northvalley High School's network was breached on November 15, 2023, leading to extensive data compromise; an unpatched personal device was the entry point.
Privacy advocate Jonathan Horowitz wrote in a September 20, 2023 op-ed that the line between protecting the network and overreaching into personal privacy is "as thin as it is critical."
A National Education Technology Council report released October 20, 2023 found most schools struggle to enforce cybersecurity best practices consistently across all students and staff.
Tina Greenfield, CIO of the Deckster School District, said on October 10, 2023 that BYOD's upfront savings are overshadowed by backend spending needed to ramp up cybersecurity.
Schools often adopt BYOD to ease budget constraints, but the hidden costs of securing an open environment can be substantial.
Students' understanding of cybersecurity is often superficial, and digital security education is weak in school curriculums.
BYOD can widen the digital divide, as students from lower-income backgrounds may bring less secure, outdated devices that also endanger the school network.
The article says inadequate policies are often exposed during crisis management, where reactive measures take precedence over proactive preparedness.
